proposals.relationship: Bailyn’s account of culture supplies a starting problem for Iriye’s exploration of connections between local mental worlds and international cultural orders.
proposals.evidence_note: The address also credits Franklin and McNeill. No mentoring claim; Bailyn’s original remains unread. Delivered 1988; published 1989.
primary_locators: Paragraphs beginning “That history” and “Ultimately”; culture discussion beginning “In addition”; notes1 and9.

proposals.relationship: Iriye invokes Curtin’s warning against self-knowledge alone when arguing that historians should communicate across cultural boundaries.
proposals.evidence_note: Specific methodological use, not career lineage. Curtin’s original address remains unread. Delivered 1988; published 1989.
primary_locators: Paragraphs beginning “Such self-criticism”, “As Philip Curtin” and “It seems to me”; note19.

proposals.relationship: Ricœur’s discussion of cultural incommunicability becomes a qualified point of engagement in Iriye’s argument for historical encounter and translation.
proposals.evidence_note: Not a refutation of Ricœur. Translator Kelbley and Ninkovich’s recommendation retain credit; original unread. Delivered 1988; published 1989.
primary_locators: Paragraph beginning “As Philip Curtin”, read through “It seems to me”; note20 names Charles A. Kelbley and Frank Ninkovich.

proposals.relationship: Iriye uses Weber’s nationalism as a contrasting example to show how cultural conceptions organize accounts of international relations.
proposals.evidence_note: He grants its relative realism but treats it as situated ideology; no formative influence inferred. Delivered 1988; published 1989.
primary_locators: Paragraphs beginning “Internationalism is clearly”, “Max Weber” and “But he defined”; note14.

proposals.relationship: Iriye uses Hobsbawm’s treatment of transnational firms in Age of Extremes as an example when explaining historians’ growing attention to non-state actors.
proposals.evidence_note: A specific historiographic resource, not personal mentoring. The same passage rejects a direct genealogy from Marxism to recent transnational historiography. Selected tool-extracted primary text, not facsimile-collated; Hobsbawm’s cited book remains unread.
primary_locators: The Rise of Global and Transnational History, printed13 paragraph beginning “By coincidence”; note15 on printed18. Permitted institutional excerpt cover dates book2012; publisher chapter copyright2013.
